4
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC Control: Analysis

We now present the analysis to obtain the performance bounds for the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC true (uncertain) Itô SDE in (
9
).
We follow a two-step approach as used for deterministic
\mathcal{L}_{1}
adaptive control analysis, see e.g.
[
30
,
104
]
.
First, in Sec.
4.1
we introduce an intermediate and non-realizable process that we call the
reference process
and obtain the performance bounds between it and the nominal (known) process.
Then, in Sec.
4.2
we analyze the performance of the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC true (uncertain) process relative to the reference process.
The last step leads us to the relative performance bounds between the true (uncertain) process and the nominal (known) process via the triangle inequality of the Wasserstein metric.

4.1
Performance Analysis: Reference Process

We begin with the definition of the reference process.

Definition 4

(Reference Process)

We say that
X^{r}_{t}
,
t\in[0,T]
, for any
T\in(0,\infty)
, is the
reference process
, if
X^{r}_{t}
is a unique strong solution to the following
reference Itô SDE
:

dX^{r}_{t}=F_{\mu}\left(t,X^{r}_{t},U^{r}_{t}\right)dt+F_{\sigma}\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)dW_{t},\quad X^{r}_{0}=x_{0}\sim\xi_{0},~\forall t\in[0,T],

(26)

where the initial condition
x_{0}\sim\xi_{0}
and the driving Brownian motion
W_{t}
are identical to those for the true (uncertain) process in (
9
) (and (
4a
)).
The
reference feedback process

U^{r}_{t}
is defined via the
reference feedback operator

\mathcal{F}_{r}
as follows:

\displaystyle U^{r}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{r}\left(X^{r}\right)(t),\quad\mathcal{F}_{r}\left(X^{r}\right)\doteq\mathcal{F}_{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\left(\Lambda_{\mu}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}\left(\cdot,X^{r}\right)\right)+\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{N},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}}\left(F^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}_{\sigma}\left(\cdot,X^{r}\right),W\right),\quad t\in[0,T],

(27)

where the operator
\mathcal{F}_{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}
is the low-pass filter defined in (
15a
), the vector field
F_{\sigma}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}
is introduced in Definition
3
, and

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{N},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}}\left(F^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}_{\sigma}\left(\cdot,X^{r}\right),W\right)(t)\doteq-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}(t-\nu)}F^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}_{\sigma}\left(\nu,X^{r}_{\nu}\right)dW_{\nu}.

(28)

Moreover, the functions
\Lambda_{\mu}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}
and
\Lambda_{\sigma}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}
are defined in Assumption
4
, and
p^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}
is defined in Assumption
5
.

Finally, similar to
\mathbb{X}_{t}
and
\mathbb{X}^{\star}_{t}
in Definition
2
, we denote by
\mathbb{X}^{r}_{t}
the
reference law (path/trajectory probability measures)
induced by the process
X^{r}_{t}
on
\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{n}\right)
, i.e.,
X^{r}_{t}\sim\mathbb{X}^{r}_{t}
.

The reference process is obtained by closing the loop of the true (uncertain) process in (
4a
) with the feedback process
U^{r}_{t}
that is composed of the filtered matched drift uncertainty
\mathcal{F}_{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\left(\Lambda_{\mu}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}\left(\cdot,X^{r}\right)\right)(t)
and the filtered
totality
of the matched diffusion vector field
\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{N},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}}\left(p^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}\left(\cdot,X^{r}\right)+\Lambda_{\sigma}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}\left(\cdot,X^{r}\right),W\right)(t)
expressed as an Itô integral with respect to the driving true Brownian motion.
Thus, the reference process is
non-realizable
since, by definition, we do not have knowledge of the epistemic uncertainties
\Lambda_{\mu}
and
\Lambda_{\sigma}
, and the aleatoric uncertainty
W
.
The reference process represents the
best achievable performance
since it quantifies, as a function of the low-pass filter bandwidth
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}
, how the system operates under the non-realizable assumption of perfect knowledge of the uncertainties.

Remark 4.1

In addition to the epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties
\Lambda_{\mu}
,
\Lambda_{\sigma}
, and
W
, the reference feedback process
U^{r}_{t}
also includes the
known
diffusion term
p\left(\cdot,X^{r}\right)
in its definition.
Therefore, the reference feedback process
U^{r}_{t}
further attempts to remove the effects of the known diffusion term
p\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)
from the reference process
X^{r}_{t}
.
The reason for the inclusion of the known diffusion term
p
is that due to the state-multiplicative nature of the term
p\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)dW_{t}
, one cannot in general disambiguate the effects of the known term
p\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)
from the total uncertainty
\int_{0}^{t}\Lambda_{\mu}\left(\nu,X^{r}_{\nu}\right)d\nu+\int_{0}^{t}\left(p\left(\nu,X^{r}_{\nu}\right)+\Lambda_{\sigma}\left(\nu,X^{r}_{\nu}\right)\right)dW_{\nu}
.

For the performance analysis of the reference process with respect to the nominal (known) process, we define the following:

Definition 5

(Joint Known (Nominal)-Reference Process)

We say that
Y_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}
,
t\in[0,T]
, for any
T\in(0,\infty)
, is the
joint known(nominal)-reference process
, if it is a unique strong solution of the following
joint known(nominal)-reference Itô SDE
on
\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathfrak{W}_{0,t}\times\mathfrak{W}^{\star}_{0,t},\mathbb{P}\right)
(see Definition
2
for the filtrations):

\displaystyle dY_{t}

\displaystyle=G_{\mu}\left(t,Y_{t}\right)dt+G_{\sigma}\left(t,Y_{t}\right)d\widehat{W}_{t},\quad t\in[0,T],\quad Y_{0}=y_{0}\sim\xi_{0}\times\xi^{\star}_{0},\quad Y_{t}\sim\mathbb{Y}_{t},

(29)

where

\displaystyle y_{0}\doteq\begin{bmatrix}x_{0}\\
x^{\star}_{0}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},\quad Y_{t}\doteq\begin{bmatrix}X^{r}_{t}\\
X^{\star}_{t}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},\quad\widehat{W}_{t}\doteq\begin{bmatrix}W_{t}\\
W^{\star}_{t}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d},

\displaystyle G_{\mu}\left(t,Y_{t}\right)\doteq\begin{bmatrix}F_{\mu}\left(t,X^{r}_{t},U^{r}_{t}\right)\\
\bar{F}_{\mu}\left(t,X^{\star}_{t}\right)\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},\quad G_{\sigma}\left(t,Y_{t}\right)\doteq\begin{bmatrix}F_{\sigma}\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)&0_{n,d}\\
0_{n,d}&\bar{F}_{\sigma}\left(t,X^{\star}_{t}\right)\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2d},

and where
\xi_{0}
and
\xi^{\star}_{0}
are the initial condition distributions and
\mathbb{Y}_{t}
denotes the law of
\left(X^{r}_{t},X^{\star}_{t}\right)
on
\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\right)
.

We obtain the desired results using the Khasminskii-type theorem
[
91
, Thm. 3.2]
.
For this purpose, we require a truncated version of (
29
) to build local solutions and extend them to the global solution using a limiting procedure.

Definition 6

(Truncated Joint Known (Nominal)-Reference Process)

We first define

U_{N}\doteq\left\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}~:~\left\|a\right\|<N\right\}\subset\subset\mathbb{R}^{2n},\quad\forall N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0},

(30)

where
\subset\subset\mathbb{R}^{2n}
denotes compact containment in
\mathbb{R}^{2n}

[
105
, Sec. A.2]
.
Next, we define the

truncated joint known(nominal)-reference Itô SDE
as

dY_{N,t}=G_{N,\mu}\left(t,Y_{N,t}\right)dt+G_{N,\sigma}\left(t,Y_{N,t}\right)d\widehat{W}_{t},\quad Y_{N,0}=Y_{0},

(31)

where, the process and the drift and diffusion vector fields are defined as

\displaystyle Y_{N,t}\doteq\begin{bmatrix}X^{r}_{N,t}\\
X^{\star}_{N,t}\end{bmatrix},\quad G_{N,\mu}\left(t,a\right)\left(G_{N,\sigma}\left(t,a\right)\right)=

\displaystyle\begin{cases}G_{\mu}\left(t,a\right)\left(G_{\sigma}\left(t,a\right)\right),\quad&~\left\|a\right\|\leq N\\
0_{2n}\left(0_{2n,2d}\right),\quad&~\left\|a\right\|\geq 2N\end{cases},\quad\forall(a,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}\times[0,T],

for any
G_{N,\mu}\left(t,a\right)
and
G_{N,\sigma}\left(t,a\right)
that are
uniformly
bounded and Lipschitz continuous for all
a\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}
and
t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
.
Similar to
Y_{t}
, we refer to
Y_{N,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}
as the
truncated joint known(nominal)-reference process
if it is a unique strong solution of (
31
).

An example of explicit construction of functions of the form
G_{N,\left\{\mu,\sigma\right\}}
can be found in
[
89
, p. 191]
.

With the setup complete, we start the analysis of the reference process by first establishing the existence and uniqueness of strong solutions of the truncated joint process.

Proposition 4.1

(Well-Posedness of (
31
))

If Assumptions
1
and
4
hold true, then for any
N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
,
Y_{N,t}
is a unique strong solution of (
31
),
\forall t\in[0,T]
, for any
T\in(0,\infty)
and is a strong Markov process
\forall t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
.
Furthermore, define
4
4
4
The stopping time
\tau_{N}
takes on the value of either the finite horizon
T
, or the first exit time of
Y_{N,t}
from set
U_{N}
.

\tau_{N}\doteq T\wedge\inf\left\{t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}~:~Y_{N,t}\notin U_{N}\right\},

(32)

where the open and bounded set
U_{N}
is defined in (
30
), for an arbitrary
N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
.
Then,
Y_{N,t}\in\mathcal{M}_{2}\left([0,\tau_{N}],\mathbb{R}^{2n}~|~\mathfrak{W}_{0,t}\times\mathfrak{W}^{\star}_{0,t}\right)
uniquely solves (
29
), in the strong sense, for all
t\in[0,\tau_{N}]
.

Proof.

See Appendix
C
.
∎

Using the well-posedness of the truncated process, we can now define the transition probability for the process as (
[
48
, Sec. 3.1]
,
[
91
, Sec. 2.9]
):

\mathbb{Y}_{N}\left(Y_{N,s},s;B,t\right)\doteq\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{N,t}\in B~|~Y_{N,s}\right),\quad\forall 0\leq s\leq t\leq T,\quad B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\right).

(33)

Next, we derive bounds on the
uniform in time
moments between the truncated versions of the reference and known (nominal) processes.

Lemma 4.1

Let the assumptions in Sec.
2.2
hold.
For an arbitrary

For any constant

5
5

Proof.

We assume w.l.o.g. that

Since

is a stopping time as well

Additionally, from Proposition

Consequently, the assumptions on the regularity of the vector fields in Sec.

We may thus apply the Itô lemma

for all

and

are defined in (

).

) and using the definitions of
\Xi^{r}
and

in (

) yields the following bound:

e^{2\lambda\tau(t)}\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\leq\mathcal{V}\left(y_{0}\right)+\Xi^{r}\left(\tau(t),Y_{N}\right)+e^{-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\tau(t)}\Xi^{r}_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Y_{N};{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right),\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},

(44)

Then, using the linearity of the expectation operator, we obtain

Finally, applying the Minkowski’s inequality to (

∎

The next result establishes moment bounds for the truncated system up to the first exit time
\tau_{N}
.

Lemma 4.2

Let the assumptions in Sec.
2.2
hold and let
{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
,
{\mathsf{p}}\in\left\{1,\dots,{\mathsf{p}}^{\star}\right\}
, be as defined in (
16a
) with
\alpha\left(X^{r}_{0},X^{\star}_{0}\right)_{2{\mathsf{p}}}=\left\|X^{r}_{0}-X^{\star}_{0}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}
, where
{\mathsf{p}}^{\star}
is defined in Assumption
3
.
If the filter bandwidth condition in (
21a
) holds with
\alpha\left(X^{r}_{0},X^{\star}_{0}\right)_{2{\mathsf{p}}}=\left\|X^{r}_{0}-X^{\star}_{0}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}
, then the truncated joint process
Y_{N,t}=\left(X^{r}_{N,t},X^{\star}_{N,t}\right)
in Definition
6
, satisfies

\displaystyle\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},\quad\forall t\in[0,\tau_{N}],

(45)

where the stopping time
\tau_{N}
is as in (
32
) for an arbitrary
N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
.

Proof.

We prove (
45
) by contradiction.
The
t
-continuity of the strong solutions
X^{r}_{N,t}
and
X^{\star}_{N,t}
on
[0,\tau_{N}]
implies that
\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}
is
t
-continuous as well.
Moreover, as we presented in (
20
), the definition of
{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
in (
16a
) implies that

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}>\left\|X^{r}_{N,0}-X^{\star}_{N,0}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}.

(46)

Then, (
46
) and the deterministic nature of
t\mapsto\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}
allow us to formulate the negation of (

) as

\displaystyle\lnot~\text{\eqref{eqn:lem:Reference:FirstExit:UB}}~:~\exists~~(deterministic)~~t^{\star}\in[0,\tau_{N}]\text{ such that }\begin{cases}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},\quad&\forall t\in[0,t^{\star})\\
\left\|X^{r}_{N,t^{\star}}-X^{\star}_{N,t^{\star}}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}={\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}.\end{cases}

(47)

Now, let
\pi_{0}
be the probability measure on
\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\right)
induced by the initial condition
Y_{N,0}=Y_{0}=\left(X^{r}_{0},X^{\star}_{0}\right)=\left(x_{0},x_{0}^{\star}\right)=y_{0}
of the truncated joint process.
Since the initial vector
Y_{N,0}=Y_{0}
is independent of the Brownian motion
\widehat{W}_{t}
, the strong solution
Y_{N,\tau(t)}
is adapted to the filtration generated by
Y_{0}
and
\widehat{W}_{t}

[
15
, Thm. 5.2.1]
.
Let us denote by
\mathbb{Y}_{N}(\cdot,t)
the law of the process
Y_{N,t}
under
Y_{N,0}\sim\pi_{0}
.
Hence,
\mathbb{Y}_{N}(\cdot,t)
is a probability measure on
\mathbb{R}^{2n}
given as

\displaystyle\mathbb{Y}_{N}(B,t)=\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{N,t}\in B\right)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{Y}_{N}\left(y_{0},0;B,t\right)\pi_{0}(dy_{0}),\quad\forall B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\right),

(48)

where the integrand is the transition probability defined in (
33
).
Then,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)\mathbb{Y}_{N}(dy,\tau(t))=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)\mathbb{Y}_{N}\left(y_{0},0;dy,\tau(t)\right)\pi_{0}(dy_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{E}_{y_{0}}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\right]\pi_{0}(dy_{0}),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},

where the last expression follows from (
37
), and
\tau(t)
is defined in (
34
).
Since we are assuming that
t^{\star}<\tau_{N}
, we have from (
34
) that
\tau^{\star}=t^{\star}
and thus
\tau(t)=t\wedge t^{\star}\in[0,t^{\star}]
, for all
t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
.
Hence, we can write the expression above as

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,t}\right)\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{E}_{y_{0}}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\right]\pi_{0}(dy_{0}),\quad t\in[0,t^{\star}].

(49)

Similarly, we can write

\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,t}\right)\right\|_{L_{{\mathsf{p}}}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,t}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\right]^{\frac{1}{{\mathsf{p}}}}=

\displaystyle\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{E}_{y_{0}}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,\tau(t)}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\right]\pi_{0}(dy_{0})\right)^{\frac{1}{{\mathsf{p}}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\left(\left\|\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\right\|_{L_{{\mathsf{p}}}}^{y_{0}}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\pi_{0}(dy_{0})\right)^{\frac{1}{{\mathsf{p}}}},\quad t\in[0,t^{\star}].

(50)

As stated above
\tau(t)\in[0,t^{\star}]
, for all
t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
.
Thus, we may use Lemma
4.1
by substituting (
35
) into (

), which produces

\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{N,t}\right)\right]\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y_{0}\right)\pi_{0}(dy_{0})+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{E}_{y_{0}}\left[e^{-2\lambda\tau(t)}\Xi^{r}\left(\tau(t),Y_{N}\right)\right]\pi_{0}(dy_{0})\\
+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{E}_{y_{0}}\left[e^{-(2\lambda+{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}})\tau(t)}\Xi^{r}_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Y_{N};{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)\right]\pi_{0}(dy_{0}),\quad\forall t\in[0,t^{\star}],

where we have used the bound
e^{-2\lambda\tau(t)}\leq 1
.
Now, recall the definition

from the statement of Lemma

. Hence, one sees that

for all

for

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\left|2\lambda-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right|}\Theta_{r}\left({\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)<\left(1-\frac{\Delta_{g}^{\perp}\Delta_{\mu}^{\perp}}{\lambda}\right){\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}^{2}-\left\|X^{r}_{0}-X^{\star}_{0}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}^{2}-\Gamma_{r}\left({\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right),

which contradicts the conclusion above in (

) that follows from the postulation in (

).
Therefore, the desired result in (

) is proved since its negation (

) leads to a contradiction.

∎

Next, we extend the strong solutions of the truncated process to the original joint process in Definition
5
.

Lemma 4.3

Let the assumptions in Sec.
2.2
hold.
Additionally, for
\alpha\left(X^{r}_{0},X^{\star}_{0}\right)_{2{\mathsf{p}}}=\left\|X^{r}_{0}-X^{\star}_{0}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}
and
{\mathsf{p}}\in\left\{1,\dots,{\mathsf{p}}^{\star}\right\}
, let
{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
be as defined in (
16a
) and let filter bandwidth condition in (
21a
) hold, where
{\mathsf{p}}^{\star}
is defined in Assumption
3
.
Then the joint process in Definition
5
admits a unique strong solution
Y_{t}=\left(X^{r}_{t},X^{\star}_{t}\right)
for all
T\in(0,\infty)
.
Furthermore, the strong solution satisfies

\displaystyle\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},\quad\forall t\in[0,T],

(70)

for any
T\in(0,\infty)
.

Proof.

We prove the existence of a unique strong solution to the reference process in Definition
4
by following the approach in
[
48
, Thm. 3.5]
,
[
89
, Thm. 5.3.1]
.
Then, along with well-posedness of the known (nominal) system in Assumption
3
, we will be able to conclude the well-posedness of the joint known (nominal)-reference process.
Let us define

\displaystyle t_{N}\doteq\inf\left\{t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}~:~Y_{N,t}\notin U_{N}\right\},

where the open and bounded set
U_{N}
is defined in (
30
), for an arbitrary
N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
.
Then, we can write the definition of
\tau_{N}
in (
32
) as

\displaystyle\tau_{N}\doteq T\wedge t_{N},

where
T\in(0,\infty)
is the horizon, and
t_{N}
is the first exit time of the truncated joint process
Y_{N,t}=\left(X^{r}_{N,t},X^{\star}_{N,t}\right)
from the set
U_{N}
.

Now, Lemma
4.2
and Jensen’s inequality allow us to conclude

\displaystyle\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2}}\leq\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},\quad\forall t\in[0,T\wedge t_{N}],

which can be further expressed as

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|^{2}\right]<{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}^{2},\quad\forall t\in[0,T\wedge t_{N}].

(71)

Furthermore, this bound and Assumption
3
allow us to conclude

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}\right\|^{2}\right]\overset{(\star)}{\leq}2\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t}-X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|^{2}\right]+2\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{\star}_{N,t}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq 2\left({\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}^{2}+\Delta_{\star}^{2}\right),\quad\forall t\in[0,T\wedge t_{N}],

(72)

where
(\star)
is due to the triangle inequality followed by
[
108
, Prop. 3.1.10 (iii)]
.

In order to establish the well-posedness of the reference process over the interval
[0,T]
it suffices to show that

\displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(t_{N}\leq T\right)=0,\quad\forall T\in(0,\infty).

Using the definition of the expectation operator, we derive the estimate

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right]=

\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{\left\{t_{N}\leq T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}+\int_{\left\{t_{N}>T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,T}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}\geq\int_{\left\{t_{N}\leq T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}.

We similarly obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}-X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right]\geq\int_{\left\{t_{N}\leq T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}}-X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}.

Combining the above two inequalities leads to

\int_{\left\{t_{N}\leq T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}+\int_{\left\{t_{N}\leq T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}}-X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}\\
\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}-X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right],\quad\forall T\in(0,\infty).

It then follows from the bounds in (
71
) and (
72
)

\int_{\left\{t_{N}\leq T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}+\int_{\left\{t_{N}\leq T\right\}}\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}}-X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}}\right\|^{2}d\mathbb{P}\\
\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}-X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq 3{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}^{2}+2\Delta_{\star}^{2},\quad\forall T\in(0,\infty).

(73)

Since
t_{N}
is the first exit time of the process
Y_{N,t}
from the set
U_{N}\subset\subset\mathbb{R}^{2n}
defined in (
30
), the stopped process
Y_{N,t_{N}}
satisfies

\displaystyle Y_{N,t_{N}}=\left(X^{r}_{N,t_{N}},X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}}\right)\in\partial U_{N},\quad\partial U_{N}=\left\{z=(z_{1},z_{2}),~z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}~|~\left\|z_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|z_{2}\right\|^{2}=N^{2}\right\}.

Therefore, we deduce from (
73
) that

\inf_{(z_{1},z_{2})\in\partial U_{N}}\left(\left\|z_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|z_{1}-z_{2}\right\|^{2}\right)\mathbb{P}\left(t_{N}\leq T\right)\\
\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}-X^{\star}_{N,t_{N}\wedge T}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq 3{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}^{2}+2\Delta_{\star}^{2},\quad\forall T\in(0,\infty).

(74)

Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, one can show that

\displaystyle\inf_{(z_{1},z_{2})\in\partial U_{N}}\left(\left\|z_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|z_{1}-z_{2}\right\|^{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\min\left\{3+\sqrt{5},3-\sqrt{5}\right\}N^{2}\geq\frac{N^{2}}{3}.

Hence, (
74
) can be developed into

\displaystyle\frac{N^{2}}{3}\mathbb{P}\left(t_{N}\leq T\right)\leq\inf_{(z_{1},z_{2})\in\partial U_{N}}\left(\left\|z_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|z_{1}-z_{2}\right\|^{2}\right)\mathbb{P}\left(t_{N}\leq T\right)\leq 3{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}^{2}+2\Delta_{\star}^{2},\quad\forall T\in(0,\infty),

which further implies that

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(t_{N}\leq T\right)\leq\frac{3}{N^{2}}\left(3{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}^{2}+2\Delta_{\star}^{2}\right),\quad\forall T\in(0,\infty).

Consequently,

\displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(t_{N}\leq T\right)=0,\quad\forall T\in(0,\infty),

(75)

which establishes the well-posedness of the reference process.
We thus define
Y_{t}=\left(X^{r}_{t},X^{\star}_{t}\right)
, where
X^{r}_{t}\doteq\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}X^{r}_{\tau_{N}(t)}
, and
\tau_{N}(t)=t\wedge\tau_{N}
.
Therefore, it follows from Fatou’s lemma
[
108
, Thm. 2.3.7]
and Lemma
4.2

\displaystyle\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}\leq\liminf_{N\rightarrow\infty}\left\|X^{r}_{\tau_{N}(t)}-X^{\star}_{\tau_{N}(t)}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},\quad\forall t\in[0,T],

for any
T\in(0,\infty)
, which establishes the desired result in (
70
).

∎

\hat{\kappa}_{r}(\delta,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},\hat{t})=e\cdot{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\hat{\varrho}_{r}}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0,0,0}\pgfsys@color@gray@stroke{0}\pgfsys@color@gray@fill{0}\log\sqrt{1/\delta},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},\hat{t}}\right)}
.

Proof.

Recall that we proved Lemma
4.2
for moments with respect to the law
\mathbb{Y}_{N}(\cdot,t):\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\right)\rightarrow[0,1]
that resulted under the arbitrary initial coupling
Y_{0}=Y_{N,0}\sim\pi_{0}
(see (
48
)).
In order to prove (
84
), we will therefore appeal to the proof of Lemma
4.2
but under the law that results from the joint process initialized under the
optimal
coupling.
Let us denote by
\pi^{\star}_{0}
the optimal coupling between the probability measures
\xi_{0}
and
\xi^{\star}_{0}
that are the respective distributions of the initial states
x_{0}
and
x^{\star}_{0}

[
29
, Chp. 1]
.
From Lemma
4.3
, the unique strong solution
Y_{t}
of the joint process exists, and is adapted to the filtration generated by
Y_{0}
and
\widehat{W}_{t}

[
15
, Thm. 5.2.1]
(initial vector
Y_{0}
is independent of the Brownian motion
\widehat{W}_{t}
).
Let us denote by
\mathbb{Y}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}(\cdot,t)
the law of the process
Y_{t}
under
Y_{0}\sim\pi^{\star}_{0}
.
Hence,
\mathbb{Y}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}(\cdot,t)
is a probability measure on
\mathbb{R}^{2n}
given as

\displaystyle\mathbb{Y}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}(B,t)=\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{t}\in B\right)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{Y}\left(y_{0},0;B,t\right)\pi^{\star}_{0}(dy_{0}),\quad\forall B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\right),

(87)

where
\mathbb{Y}\left(y_{0},0;B,t\right)
denotes the transition probability for the process
Y_{t}
, initialized from
y_{0}

[
48
, Sec. 3.1]
.
Then, for
\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{t}\right)=\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|^{2}
we can define

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{t}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\mathbb{Y}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}(dy,t)=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\mathbb{Y}\left(y_{0},0;dy,t\right)\pi^{\star}_{0}(dy_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{t}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}~|~Y_{0}=y_{0}\right]\pi^{\star}_{0}(dy_{0})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathbb{E}_{y_{0}}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{t}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\right]\pi^{\star}_{0}(dy_{0}),

(88)

for
t\in[0,T]
.
Note that if we were to replace the optimal initial coupling
\pi^{\star}_{0}
with an arbitrary coupling
\pi_{0}
, then (
4.1
) yields (
49
) and (
4.1
).
Since
\pi^{\star}_{0}
is the optimal coupling between the initial measures
\xi_{0}
and
\xi^{\star}_{0}
, it follows from the definition of the Wasserstein distance that

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y_{0}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\pi^{\star}_{0}(dy_{0})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\left\|x_{0}-x^{\star}_{0}\right\|^{2{\mathsf{p}}}\pi^{\star}_{0}(dx_{0},dx_{0}^{\star})=\mathsf{W}_{2{\mathsf{p}}}\left(\xi_{0},\xi^{\star}_{0}\right)^{2{\mathsf{p}}}.

We can thus follow the analysis in Lemma
4.2
for the law
\mathbb{Y}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}(\cdot,t)
of the joint process
Y_{t}
up to the stopping time
T
and obtain

\displaystyle\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}^{\pi^{\star}_{0}}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|^{2{\mathsf{p}}}\right]^{\frac{1}{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},\quad\forall t\in[0,T],

(89)

where
{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}
is defined in (
16a
) with
\alpha\left(X^{r}_{0},X^{\star}_{0}\right)_{2{\mathsf{p}}}=\mathsf{W}_{2{\mathsf{p}}}\left(\xi_{0},\xi^{\star}_{0}\right)
.
We now follow the approach in
[
109
]
and, using (
87
), define the measure
\pi_{t}=\mathbb{Y}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}(\cdot,t)
.
It then follows from (
4.1
)

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|^{2{\mathsf{p}}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Y_{t}\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\mathbb{Y}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}(dy,t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\pi_{t}(dy).

Since
\pi_{t}
is not necessarily the optimal coupling between the state distributions
\mathbb{X}^{r}_{t}
and
\mathbb{X}_{t}^{\star}
, we reason that

\displaystyle\mathsf{W}_{2{\mathsf{p}}}\left(\mathbb{X}^{r}_{t},\mathbb{X}_{t}^{\star}\right)^{2{\mathsf{p}}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\pi^{\star}_{t}(dy)\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\mathcal{V}\left(y\right)^{\mathsf{p}}\pi_{t}(dy)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\star}_{0}}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|^{2{\mathsf{p}}}\right],\quad\forall t\in[0,T],

where
\pi^{\star}_{t}
denotes the optimal coupling between the state distributions
\mathbb{X}^{r}_{t}
and
\mathbb{X}_{t}^{\star}
.
Substituting the above into (
89
) then establishes (
84a
).
The bound in (
84b
) follows
mutatis mutandis
from the analysis above and the proof of Proposition
4.2
.

Next, for any
\kappa\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
, we can use the Markov’s inequality
[
108
, Cor. 3.1.2]
and Lemma
4.3
to obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|\geq\kappa\right)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|^{2{\mathsf{p}}}\right]}{\kappa^{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<\left(\frac{{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}}{\kappa}\right)^{2{\mathsf{p}}},\quad\forall(t,{\mathsf{p}})\in[0,T]\times[1,{\mathsf{p}}^{\star}].

By setting
{\mathsf{p}}=\log\sqrt{\frac{1}{\delta}}
and
\kappa=e\cdot{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}
, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|X^{r}_{t}-X^{\star}_{t}\right\|\geq\kappa_{r}(\delta)\right)<\delta,\quad\forall t\in[0,T],

thus establishing (
86a
).
The proof of (
86b
) follows
mutatis mutandis
by using the uniform ultimate bound from Proposition
4.2
.

∎

(95)

where
{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
is the
sampling period
and

, with

We collectively refer to

Our goal in this section is to establish the performance of the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC closed-loop true (uncertain) process in (
90
) relative to the reference process in Definition
4
.
For this purpose, we provide the following:

Definition 8

(True (Uncertain)-Reference Error Process)

Consider the true process
X_{t}
and the reference process
X^{r}_{t}\sim\mathbb{X}^{r}_{t}
in Definitions
7
and
4
, respectively.
We say that
Z_{t}
,
t\in[0,T]
, for any
T\in(0,\infty)
, is the
true (uncertain)-reference joint process
, if it is a unique strong solution of the following
true (uncertain)-reference joint Itô SDE
on
\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathfrak{W}_{0,t},\mathbb{P}\right)
:

\displaystyle dZ_{t}

\displaystyle=J_{\mu}\left(t,Z_{t}\right)dt+J_{\sigma}\left(t,Z_{t}\right)dW_{t},\quad t\in[0,T],\quad Z_{0}=0,\quad Z_{t}\sim\mathbb{Z}_{t},

(97)

where

\displaystyle Z_{t}\doteq X_{t}-X^{r}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\quad J_{\mu}\left(t,Z_{t}\right)\doteq F_{\mu}\left(t,X_{t},U_{\mathcal{L}_{1},t}\right)-F_{\mu}\left(t,X^{r}_{t},U^{r}_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

\displaystyle J_{\sigma}\left(t,Z_{t}\right)\doteq F_{\sigma}\left(t,X_{t}\right)-F_{\sigma}\left(t,X^{r}_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

Remark 4.2

The definition of the joint process above between the true (uncertain) process and the reference process is
not
a direct analogue to the joint known (nominal)-reference process in Definition
5
.
The reason is that the true (uncertain) process and the reference process are driven by the identical Brownian motion
W_{t}
and share the same initial condition
x_{0}\sim\xi_{0}
.
This is in contrast to the joint known (nominal)-reference process in Definition
5
, where the known (nominal) process and the reference process are driven by
independent Brownian motions

W^{\star}_{t}
and
W_{t}
and have
distinct initial data

x_{0}\sim\xi_{0}
and
x^{\star}_{0}\sim\xi^{\star}_{0}
, respectively.
Recall from our discussion after Definition
4
that the reference process is
not-realizable
and represents the best achievable performance, and thus we designed the reference process to be driven by the identical Brownian motion and share the same initial condition as the true (uncertain) process.

Similar to the truncated joint known (nominal)-reference process in Definition
6
, we require the following:

Definition 9

(Truncated Joint True (Uncertain)-Reference Process)

Let

\widetilde{U}_{N}\doteq\left\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}~:~\left\|a\right\|<N\right\}\subset\subset\mathbb{R}^{n},\quad\forall N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}.

(98)

Next, we define the
truncated joint true (uncertain)-reference Itô SDE
as

dZ_{N,t}=J_{N,\mu}\left(t,Z_{N,t}\right)dt+J_{N,\sigma}\left(t,Z_{N,t}\right)dW_{t},\quad Z_{N,0}=Z_{0}=0,

(99)

where, the process and the drift and diffusion vector fields are defined as

\displaystyle Z_{N,t}\doteq X_{N,t}-X^{r}_{N,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\quad J_{N,\mu}\left(t,a\right)\left(J_{N,\sigma}\left(t,a\right)\right)=

\displaystyle\begin{cases}J_{\mu}\left(t,a\right)\left(J_{\sigma}\left(t,a\right)\right),\quad&~\left\|a\right\|\leq N\\
0_{n}\left(0_{n,d}\right),\quad&~\left\|a\right\|\geq 2N\end{cases},

for all
(a,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T]
, where
J_{N,\mu}\left(t,a\right)
and
J_{N,\sigma}\left(t,a\right)
are any
uniformly
Lipschitz continuous maps for all
a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
and
t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
.
Similar to
Z_{t}
, we refer to
Z_{N,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
as the
truncated joint known(nominal)-reference process
if it is a unique strong solution of (
99
).

We begin by establishing the uniqueness and existence of strong solutions for the truncated joint true (uncertain)-reference process.

Proposition 4.3

(Well-Posedness of (
99
))

If Assumptions
1
and
4
hold, then for any
N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
,
Z_{N,t}
is a unique strong solution of (
99
),
\forall t\in[0,T]
, for any
T\in(0,\infty)
and is a strong Markov process
\forall t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
.
Furthermore, define
6
6
6
The stopping time
\tau_{N}
takes on the value of either the finite horizon
T
, or the first exit time of
Z_{N,t}
from set
\widetilde{U}_{N}
.

\tau_{N}\doteq T\wedge\inf\left\{t\in[0,T]~:~Z_{N,t}\notin\widetilde{U}_{N}\right\},

(100)

where the open and bounded set
\widetilde{U}_{N}
is defined in (
98
), for an arbitrary
N\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
.
Then,
Z_{N,t}
uniquely solves (
97
), in the strong sense, for all

.

Proof.

See Appendix
D
.

Remark 4.3

Recall that
\tau_{N}
in (
32
), Proposition
4.1
, denotes the first exit time of the process
Y_{N,t}
from the set
U_{N}\subset\subset\mathbb{R}^{2n}
.
Similarly, with an abuse of notation and from this point onward,
\tau_{N}
in (
100
) denotes the first exit time of the process
Z_{N,t}
from the set
\widetilde{U}_{N}\subset\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}
.

Using the well-posedness of the truncated process, we can now define the following transition probability:

\mathbb{Z}_{N}\left(Z_{N,s},s;B,t\right)\doteq\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{N,t}\in B~|~Z_{N,s}\right),\quad\forall 0<s\leq t\leq T,\quad B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{n}\right).

(101)

With an abuse of notation, let us also denote the law of the process
Z_{N,t}
by
\mathbb{Z}_{N}
.
Thus,
\mathbb{Z}_{N}(\cdot,t)
is a probability measure on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
given as

\displaystyle\mathbb{Z}_{N}(B,t)=\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{N,t}\in B\right)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\mathbb{Z}_{N}\left(z_{0},0;B,t\right)\mathbb{P}(dz_{0}),\quad\forall B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{n}\right),

where
\mathbb{P}(z_{0})
denotes the distribution of the initial condition
Z_{N,0}
.
Hence, for any Borel measurable function
a:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[a\left(Z_{N,t}\right)\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}a(z)\mathbb{Z}_{N}(dz,t)=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}a(z)\mathbb{Z}_{N}\left(z_{0},0;dz,t\right)\mathbb{P}(dz_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[a\left(Z_{N,t}\right)~|~Z_{N,0}=z_{0}\right]\mathbb{P}(dz_{0}).

However, since
\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{N,0}=0\right)=1
, the previous expression can be written as

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[a\left(Z_{N,t}\right)\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[a\left(Z_{N,t}\right)~|~Z_{N,0}=z_{0}\right]\delta_{0}(dz_{0})=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[a\left(Z_{N,t}\right)~|~Z_{N,0}=0\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}a(z)\mathbb{Z}_{N}\left(0,0;dz,t\right),

(102)

where
\delta_{0}
is the Dirac measure supported on
0\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
.
Hence, the following analysis uses the total expectation as it is identical to the expectation conditioned on the zero initial condition.

uniform in time

\phi_{\sigma^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.3858pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\resizebox{2.8858pt}{2.25pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}}
in (
112
), we obtain

\displaystyle\phi_{\mu^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.3858pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\resizebox{2.8858pt}{2.25pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu}\right)+\phi_{U_{\mu}}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu};{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)=\frac{2\lambda}{2\lambda-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}}\partial\mathcal{V}\left(Z_{N,\nu}\right)^{\top}g(\nu)\mathring{\Lambda}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}_{\mu}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu}\right),

\displaystyle\phi_{\sigma^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.3858pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\resizebox{2.8858pt}{2.25pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu}\right)+\phi_{U_{\sigma}}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu};{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)=\frac{2\lambda}{2\lambda-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}}\partial\mathcal{V}\left(Z_{N,\nu}\right)^{\top}g(\nu)\mathring{F}^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.4pt}{\resizebox{5.91821pt}{6.29999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.98pt}{\resizebox{4.27098pt}{4.40999pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.57098pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}_{\sigma}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu}\right).

Substituting into (
113
) thus produces

\int_{0}^{\tau(t)}e^{2\lambda\nu}\left(\left[\phi_{U}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu}\right)+\phi_{\mu^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.3858pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\resizebox{2.8858pt}{2.25pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu}\right)\right]d\nu+\phi_{\sigma^{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.0pt}{\resizebox{5.31639pt}{4.5pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\resizebox{3.3858pt}{3.15pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\resizebox{2.8858pt}{2.25pt}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\parallel$}}}}}}}\left(\nu,Z_{N,\nu}\right)dW_{\nu}\right)\\
=e^{-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\tau(t)}\int_{0}^{\tau(t)}\left(\mathcal{U}_{\mu}\left(\tau(t),\nu,Z_{N};{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)d\nu+\mathcal{U}_{\sigma}\left(\tau(t),\nu,Z_{N};{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)dW_{\nu}\right),\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},

where
\mathcal{U}_{\mu}
and
\mathcal{U}_{\sigma}
are defined in (
109
).
Substituting the above expression for the last integral on the right hand side of (
112
) and using the definitions of
\Xi
,
\Xi_{\mathcal{U}}
, and
\widetilde{\Xi}_{\mathcal{U}}
in (
107
) yields the following bound:

\displaystyle e^{2\lambda\tau(t)}\mathcal{V}\left(Z_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\leq\Xi\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right)+e^{-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\tau(t)}\Xi_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right)+\widetilde{\Xi}_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right),\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},

which implies

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\left(Z_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\leq e^{-2\lambda\tau(t)}\Xi\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right)+e^{-(2\lambda+{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}})\tau(t)}\Xi_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right)+e^{-2\lambda\tau(t)}\widetilde{\Xi}_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right),\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.

(114)

Then, using the linearity of the expectation operator, we obtain

\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{V}\left(Z_{N,\tau(t)}\right)\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-2\lambda\tau(t)}\Xi\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right)\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-(2\lambda+{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}})\tau(t)}\Xi_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right)\right]\\
+\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-2\lambda\tau(t)}\widetilde{\Xi}_{\mathcal{U}}\left(\tau(t),Z_{N}\right)\right],\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},

which establishes (
105
).
Finally, applying Minkowski’s inequality to (
114
) for
{\mathsf{p}}\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}
yields the bound in (
106
), thus concluding the proof.

∎

We next derive bounds on the conditional moments of the truncated joint true (uncertain)-reference process up to the stopping time
\tau_{N}
.

Lemma 4.6

Let the assumptions in Sec.
2.2
hold and let
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
,

), where

in Definition

\displaystyle\left\|X_{N,t}-X^{r}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}},\quad\forall t\in[0,\tau_{N}],

Proof.

We prove (

The

on

We have from Definitions

-
9
that

Thus, since
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}>0

\displaystyle\lnot~\text{\eqref{eqn:lem:True:FirstExit:UB}}~:~\exists~~(deterministic)~~t^{\star}\in[0,\tau_{N}]\text{ such that }\begin{cases}\left\|X_{N,t}-X^{r}_{N,t}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}},\quad&\forall t\in[0,t^{\star}),\\
\left\|X_{N,t^{\star}}-X^{r}_{N,t^{\star}}\right\|_{L_{2{\mathsf{p}}}}={\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}.\end{cases}

(116)

Now,
\tau(t)=(t\wedge t^{\star})\in[0,t^{\star}]
, for all

because

in (

and

for all

for

where we have defined the following for

4.3
Discussion

A few critical points merit a discussion.

Tighter High-probability Guarantees:

Recall the definition
{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{)}}={\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}
from (
17
), where
{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}
are defined in (
16
).
The terms
{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}
depend on the moment
{\mathsf{p}}\in\left\{1,\dots,{\mathsf{p}}^{\star}\right\}
, through the constants presented in Appendix
A.1
.
It is easy to establish that
\left\{{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}\right\}\in\mathcal{O}\left({\mathsf{p}}^{2}\right)
, as
{\mathsf{p}}\rightarrow\infty
.
It then follows that the pathwise uniform bound
\kappa(\delta)
in (
147a
), Thm.
4.1
, satisfies
\kappa(\delta)\in\mathcal{O}\left(\log^{2}\sqrt{1/\delta}\right)
, as
\delta\downarrow 0
.
It can be similarly shown that the pathwise uniform ultimate bound
\hat{\kappa}(\delta,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},\hat{t})
in (
147b
) is also of the same order in
\delta\in(0,1)
.

The order
2

polylog
(polylogarithmic) dependence of the bounds
\kappa
and
\hat{\kappa}
on the probability of violation
\delta\in(0,1)
implies much tighter bounds for small
\delta
when compared to bounds resulting from using up to only the first two moments.
For example, if the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC controller could only guarantee bounds up to
{\mathsf{p}}=1
(moments up to
2{\mathsf{p}}
), then
\kappa\in\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{1/\delta}\right)
, as
\delta\downarrow 0
, which leads to substantially large bounds for small
\delta
.
As an example, for
\delta=10^{-10}
,
\log^{2}\sqrt{1/\delta}=132.55
, while
\sqrt{1/\delta}=10^{5}
.

Generalization of the Deterministic Design and Performance:

As discussed in Remark
3.2
, the filter bandwidth conditions (
21
) are
\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}}\right)
, as
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\rightarrow\infty
.
For the purposes of this discussion, we may interpret the order of
1/{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}
on which the bandwidth functions depend as the ‘strength’ of the controller’s ability.
In the absence of the diffusion vector fields, however, one sees that

\displaystyle\left\{\frac{1}{\left|2\lambda-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right|}\Theta_{r}\left({\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right),\,\frac{1}{\left|2\lambda-{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right|}\Theta_{a}\left({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}},{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}},{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)\right\}\in\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}}\right),

as
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\rightarrow\infty
, which represents a ‘stronger’ ability of the controller.
Indeed, the
\mathcal{O}\left(1/{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right)
dependence of the bandwidth conditions is consistent with our previous results on
\mathcal{L}_{1}
adaptive controller design for deterministic systems, see e.g.
[
104
,
110
]
.
It can be similarly shown that the functions
\Upsilon_{a_{i}}
,
i\in\left\{1,2,3\right\}
, that define the sampling period condition in (
24
) satisfy

\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{3}\Upsilon_{a_{i}}\left({\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho^{\prime}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{)}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}};{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)\in\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}}\right),\text{ as }{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\downarrow 0.

Instead, in the absence of the diffusion terms, the function above belongs to
\mathcal{O}\left({\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)
, as
{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\downarrow 0
, which is similar to piecewise constant adaptation laws utilized in the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
adaptive controller for deterministic systems, see e.g.
[
111
,
112
]
.
Finally, in the absence of diffusion terms, and unmatched uncertainties, i.e., deterministic system subject to only matched uncertainties, we recover definitions of the bounds
{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{\varrho_{r}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{0.18,1,0.7}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.18,1,0.7}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.82}{0}{0.30}{0}\bm{)}}
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\varrho_{a}(}}{\mathsf{p}}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{)}}
that are consistent with our previous results on deterministic systems in
[
104
]
.

These observations lead to the conclusion that the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC control generalizes
\mathcal{L}_{1}
adaptive control design for deterministic systems, in both design requirements and performance guarantees.

5
Conclusion

We provide
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC methodology that allows the synthesis of controllers that can guarantee distributionally robust control on uncertain nonlinear processes.
The
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC is based on the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
adaptive control architecture.
The robustness guarantees ensured by the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC feedback are in the form of Wasserstein ambiguity sets centered on nominal state distributions with
a priori
known radius.
The class of uncertain nonlinear systems for which the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-DRAC controller is applicable consists of systems with unbounded epistemic uncertainties in both drift and diffusion: a significantly larger class of systems than currently considered for similar synthesis problems in the literature.

Proposition A.1

The mapping
\xi\mapsto\check{\Upsilon}\left(\xi;{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)
,
\check{\Upsilon}\in\left\{\Upsilon^{\prime}_{1},\Upsilon^{\prime}_{2},\Upsilon^{\prime}_{3},\widetilde{\Upsilon}^{-},\Upsilon^{-},\mathring{\Upsilon}\right\}
, is non-decreasing over
\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
, i.e.

\displaystyle\check{\Upsilon}\left(\xi_{1};{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)\leq\check{\Upsilon}\left(\xi_{2};{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right),\quad\forall\left(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times\mathbb{R}_{>0},\quad\xi_{1}\leq\xi_{2}.

(A.20)

Furthermore, the following limits are satisfied for any fixed
\left\{\xi,{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}}\right\}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{R}_{>0}

\displaystyle\lim_{{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\downarrow 0}\left\{\widetilde{\Upsilon}^{-},\Upsilon^{-},\Upsilon^{\prime}_{1},\Upsilon^{\prime}_{2},\Upsilon^{\prime}_{3}\right\}\left(\xi;{\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)=0.

\displaystyle\lim_{{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\downarrow 0}{\Delta}_{\mu_{i}}\left({\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)=0,\quad\lim_{{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\downarrow 0}{\Delta}_{\sigma_{i}}\left({\mathsf{p}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{1,0,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0}{1}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0}{1}{0}{0}\bm{\omega}},{\color[rgb]{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\definecolor[named]{pgfstrokecolor}{rgb}{0.0600000000000001,0.46,1}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@stroke{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\pgfsys@color@cmyk@fill{0.94}{0.54}{0}{0}\bm{T_{s}}}\right)=0,\quad i\in\left\{1,2,3\right\}.

(A.25)

The claim in (
A.21
) then follows by applying the above limits to the mappings in (
A.18
) and (
A.19
).

∎

B
Technical Results

Remark B.1

The results that we present in this appendix consider functions belonging to
\mathcal{M}_{2}^{loc}\left(\mathcal{X}~|~\mathcal{F}_{t}\right)
, for some finite-dimensional space
\mathcal{X}
and filtration
\mathcal{F}_{t}
,
t\in[0,T]
.
However, it is straightforward to see that the results hold for the more general space
\mathcal{M}_{2}\left([0,T];\mathcal{X}~|~\mathcal{F}_{t}\right)
.
In fact, Appendices
C
and
D
invoke the following results since they also hold over
\mathcal{M}_{2}\left([0,\tau\wedge T];\mathcal{X}~|~\mathcal{F}_{t}\right)
, where
\tau
is any stopping-time.

We begin with the following result that is a multidimensional version of the stochastic integration by parts formula in
[
91
, Thm. 1.6.5]
.

Lemma B.1

Consider any
L\in\mathcal{M}_{2}^{loc}\left(\mathbb{R}^{l\times l^{\prime}}|\mathfrak{F}_{t}\right)
and
S\in\mathcal{M}_{2}^{loc}\left(\mathbb{R}^{l^{\prime}\times n_{q}}|\mathfrak{F}_{t}\right)
, for some filtration
\mathfrak{F}_{t}
on
\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}\right)
.
Then, for any
n_{q}
-dimensional
\mathfrak{F}_{t}
-adapted Brownian motion
Q_{t}
, we have that

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{\nu}L(\nu)S(\beta)dQ_{\beta}d\nu=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\nu}^{t}L(\beta)S(\nu)d\beta dQ_{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{l},

(B.1a)

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\nu}^{t}L(\nu)S(\beta)dQ_{\beta}d\nu=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{\nu}L(\beta)S(\nu)d\beta dQ_{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{l},

(B.1b)

for all
t\in[0,T]
.

Proof.

We provide a proof for (
B.1a
) only since (
B.1b
) can be established
mutatis mutandis
.
We begin by defining

\displaystyle\hat{L}(\varsigma)\doteq\int_{0}^{\varsigma}L(\beta)d\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times l^{\prime}},\quad\varsigma\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.

(B.2)

As a consequence of the above definition, we have that

\displaystyle\int_{\nu}^{t}L(\beta)d\beta=\int_{0}^{t}L(\beta)d\beta-\int_{0}^{\nu}L(\beta)d\beta\doteq\hat{L}(t)-\hat{L}(\nu)\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times l^{\prime}},\quad 0\leq\nu\leq t\leq T.

(B.3)

Using the expression above, we may write the right hand side of (
B.1a
) as

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\nu}^{t}L(\beta)S(\nu)d\beta dQ_{\nu}=\int_{0}^{t}\left(\int_{\nu}^{t}L(\beta)d\beta\right)S(\nu)dQ_{\nu}=\int_{0}^{t}\left(\hat{L}(t)-\hat{L}(\nu)\right)S(\nu)dQ_{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{l},

which can further be re-written as

\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\nu}^{t}L(\beta)S(\nu)d\beta dQ_{\nu}\\
&=\int_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\left(\hat{L}_{1}(t)-\hat{L}_{1}(\nu)\right)S(\nu)dQ_{\nu}&\cdots&\left(\hat{L}_{l}(t)-\hat{L}_{l}(\nu)\right)S(\nu)dQ_{\nu}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\end{aligned}\\
=\sum_{i=1}^{l^{\prime}}\int_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\left(\hat{L}_{1,i}(t)-\hat{L}_{1,i}(\nu)\right)S_{i}(\nu)dQ_{\nu}&\cdots&\left(\hat{L}_{l,i}(t)-\hat{L}_{l,i}(\nu)\right)S_{i}(\nu)dQ_{\nu}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{l},

(B.4)

where
\hat{L}_{1,\cdots,l}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times l^{\prime}}
and
S_{1,\cdots,l^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times n_{q}}
are the rows of
\hat{L}(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times l^{\prime}}
defined in (
B.2
) and
